speechtext:
1.	What has been done since last session to establish a maritime commission in the province of Ontario, for the river St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes?
2.	What facilities and other aids to navigation have been considered by the government since last session and what action has been taken?

maintopic: MARITIME COMMISSION FOR ST. LAWRENCE AND GREAT LAKES  AIDS TO NAVIGATION
speechtext:
1.	The jurisdiction of the Canadian maritime commission extends to the great lakes and St. Lawrence river as well as to the east and west coasts.
2.	Since last session ten lighthouses and six fog alarms have been improved and twenty-four unlighted buoys have been placed. One improved combined light and fog alarm station is now under construction. A new lifeboat for the east coast is under construction. At Montreal, Toronto, and Midland, equipment has been installed to provide radiophone communication service for shipping on very high frequency to supplement the service now being provided on medium frequency. Action has been taken to provide duplex terminal equipment for stations at Midland and Port Burwell,' Ontario, and Father Point, Quebec, in order that persons on board radiophone-equipped ships may establish direct telephone contact with any telephone subscriber on shore; all other stations on the Great Lakes and at Montreal and Quebec already have been equipped for this service.
In addition the 1949 program involves the establishment of nine beacon lights, thirteen lighted buoys, and three radar reflectors and the installation of a radiophone at Parry Sound.
An answer furnished last year indicated the numerous aids to navigation already in operation and pointed out the requirements of the Canada Shipping Act with respect to the carrying of life-saving appliances and equipment on ships and the yearly inspection of hulls and equipment by steamship inspectors.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES    QUESTION AS TO EXTENSION    CORRESPONDENCE BETWEEN GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
The hon. member telephoned notice of his question to my office about fifteen minutes ago, and I have not had time to go into it as fully as I should like to. I can, however, tell him this. The notes exchanged between the United States government and the Secretary of State for External Affairs I presume are privileged documents, and I would doubt whether the Secretary of State for External Affairs would wish to table them. That is, however, a matter for him to decide.
344	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry
As to the agreement which has been signed between Canada and the United States covering air traffic rights, I can see no objection to its being tabled, and I shall ask my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs to have that done.
As to the extension of thirty days, to which my hon. friend referred, of certain air traffic rights which lines of the United States have at Gander, these rights have been extended following discussions with the United States authorities, who have assured us that they are doing everything they can to implement the agreement signed between Canada and the United States.

The plans for the transfer of headquarters group of the operations department of Trans-Canada Air Lines from Winnipeg to Montreal will have been fully implemented by Monday, October 3. Office accommodation has been completed on schedule in the international aviation building, Dorchester street, Montreal, even to. the installation of telephones, so that the move should involve little interruption to the work of the air line.

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO PROCEDURE WHEN PARLIAMENT IN SESSION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO PROCEDURE WHEN PARLIAMENT IN SESSION
speechtext:
few days ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) intimated to the house some changes in the regulations with regard to the importation of fruit and vegetables. That seems to be the proper procedure when the house is sitting. I noticed this morning that a press release was issued yesterday by the Department of Trade and Commerce, announcing important changes in various tariff items, and in foreign exchange regulations affecting the steel industry. I am wondering why the
[Mr. Chevrier.l

announcement was made by a statement to the press, when the house is sitting, rather than to the house in the first instance so that members might have an opportunity of asking questions if they wished to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO PROCEDURE WHEN PARLIAMENT IN SESSION
speechtext:
I made a statement in the house with regard to fruit and vegetables. That was done because it is a matter in which there is wide public interest. As to changes in connection with the emergency exchange regulations, I may say that I do not make a statement in the house if they are of a more or less routine character. I felt, however, that the matter of fruit and vegetables was one of general interest.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Dion in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Resolved, that a sum not exceeding $114,516,603.83, being one-twelfth of the amount of each of the several items to be voted, except items 43, 419 and 452, as set forth in the main estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1950, laid before the House of Commons at the present session of parliament; a sum not exceeding $2,613,651.00, being one-twelfth of the several items to be voted, as set out in the supplementary estimates (Newfoundland); a sum not exceeding $5,876,758.33, being one-twelfth of the several items to be voted as set out in the further supplementary estimates, and a sum not exceeding $468,750.00, being five-twelfths of item 907 to be voted as set out in the further supplementary estimates laid before the House of Commons at the present session of parliament, be granted to His Majesty on account for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1950.
He said: Before you put the resolution, Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might give just a word of explanation as to the interim supply which I am asking for.
The bill which will be founded on this resolution will ask for an additional one-twelfth of all the items contained in the main estimates, one-twelfth of all the items in what are referred to as the Newfoundland supplementaries, one-twelfth of all the items in the further supplementaries which I tabled the day before yesterday, and five-twelfths of one item, item 907 in those other supplementaries, which relates to the additional work of the Fraser valley diking board. I am informed that the work is proceeding rapidly and that the amount asked for will be required.
Members of the committee who were here in the last parliament will recall that six months' interim supply was voted before parliament was dissolved in the latter part of April. Consequently that supply will run out on September 30, which is tomorrow. The form of the bill which will be placed

before the house is exactly the same as the other supply bills which have been passed by the house from time to time. The passing of the bill will not result in the passing of the full amount of any item, and will not prejudice the rights and privileges of members to criticize and discuss items in the estimates which will come up for consideration from time to time during the remainder of the session. Of course I give the usual undertaking that such rights and privileges will be respected, and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as a result of the passing of the proposed measure.
In asking for only one-twelfth of the total amount, does the minister believe that all the estimates will be through by the end of next month?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hope springs eternal. If we do not get them through by then, I shall have to come back before the end of October.

Mr. Chairman, the committee will be only conducting a post mortem on these expenditures, as we understand it. The time is coming when there should be some reduction. I speak on behalf of the businessmen of the country. The government made that promise in the last election campaign. I fail to see why the House of Commons is sanctioning this interim supply for a period which will extend practically to the end of October, with the House of Commons simply holding a post mortem on these expenditures. I think we are going too far. What is the House of Commons for if not to check up on expenditures? It was on that principle, taxation without representation, that the American colonies seceded from the mother country. Yet here we are, a long time afterwards, adopting the same principle. I wish to protest against it, as I have done on other occasions.
May I ask the Minister of Finance what is the total amount that is being voted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. The
amount is set forth in the resolution which the chairman will read in a moment. It is $114,516,603.83, plus $2,613,651, plus $5,876,758.33, plus $468,750.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What does that add up to?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The total of the item asked for by the hon. member for Eglinton is $123,475,763.16.

Included in the figure which is being asked for by the Minister of Finance are several items coming under the jurisdiction of the Secretary of State. Because the patent office of Canada comes under that department I want to raise a question which I could not very well raise on the orders of
Interim Supply
the day. I shall be brief, because the minister is new to the house.
First of all I wish to welcome the hon. gentleman-it is the first opportunity I have had to do so-and to wish him well in the work which lies ahead. At the same time I want to give him a word of caution. The question of the great arrears of work in the patent office is one of which he had better be made aware at the very first opportunity, and I think this is that opportunity.
As the Chairman knows, by a recommendation of a committee of this house the patent fees were raised from $15 to $25 on the original application and a similar amount when the patent is issued. That increase was decided on largely because the committee recommended that these patents be printed. I am told that for some considerable time the printing has been paid for with these additional fees, but the work is still far behind. In addition, the quarters, while more nearly adequate than they were before, still fall short of meeting the need which is evident all along the line.
Some few years ago it was said that there were some 30,000 patents still to be dealt with. I am informed that the patents are running somewhat behind, even in respect to current applications. The commissioner and his staff, inadequate as it is, are unable to handle the backlog because they cannot keep up with the current applications.
For the benefit of new members it ought to be said that the patent office is an open house for the public. In addition it has significance far beyond our domestic scene, because of international implications. From Canada's point of view it is not good business to have the patent office, which has international significance, so far behind in its work. As the minister will understand, I am not raising this question to criticize him or to criticize those who have been in charge of the patent office. I am merely indicating a concentrated drive ought to be made by the minister, backed by the government, to see to it that we get in line with the British patent office and with the United States patent office. Since the war quite a length of time has elapsed, and this country cannot afford to have anything but a good reputation when it is dealing with a matter of this kind.
The patent office of course has definitely a link with business generally in the countl'y. I am quite sure that business will expect that a government department will at least keep abreast of the times. I am throwing this out only as a suggestion; perhaps it will not bear close scrutiny. In any event, in the United States and in Britain one finds the patent office under the jurisdiction of the department of commerce. It is closely related

Interim Supply
to trade and commerce. In the United Kingdom I understand it is under the board of trade, because of the fact that it is related to business and commerce. When I say this I am not reflecting upon the minister. Perhaps the government might give consideration to relating patent work with the department with which it is most closely allied, and following the precedent which has been established in those other two countries.
I have not given the matter much consideration; perhaps there are good reasons why the patent office should not come under the Department of Trade and Commerce. In any event my main reason for raising the question now is to impress upon the new minister and upon the government the necessity of seeing to it that a concentrated drive is made to bring the patent office up to date and to provide the facilities and the staff which are so urgently needed to do the job.

On the orders of the day I asked a question about announcements of policy by press releases when parliament is sitting. The answer given by the Minister of Finance was quite satisfactory as far as it went. I think that matters of small import to a community can be dealt with in that way. The reason I ask the question is that a press statement issued yesterday involved an important government decision and was of wide public interest. There may be a good reason why, in order to conserve foreign exchange, the policy announced in the press release should be approved. Hon. members might be interested in the list of the materials involved. They comprise pig iron, ingots, blooms, billets, bars, rods, plates, sheets and forgings. All these items will now be imported under permit to be issued under the foreign exchange regulations. In regard to an important group of items such as this it would be well to have the announcement made in the house in order that hon. members might have an opportunity of knowing what was being done in such an important matter. Sometimes press releases are tucked away in the corner of a newspaper and we do not see them. That was my reason for asking the question. I was making the suggestion that when an announcement touching very important imports of this description is made, at a time when the house is sitting, perhaps it would be well to have it made hi the house rather than to have it made public by way of a press release.

Mr. Chairman, I admit at once that the issuance of that statement was an error. It was a steel controller order made under wartime legislation, and it came to me for approval. It was not effective until October 1, and I fully intended to make the

announcement in the house. I was as much surprised as the hon. member to read it in the press. However, since the mistake had been made, I saw no purpose in making the announcement in the house.
Did the Minister of Finance indicate what proportion of the further supplementary estimates is included in the sum for which he is asking today?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am asking today for one-twelfth of the new supplementary estimates, along with the other items to which I referred.

Mr. Chairman, as there are funds in this resolution which come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, I should like to draw his attention to a question I raised in the house on September 20, when I asked him about the plight of certain imperial pensioners in Canada brought about by the devaluation of the pound.
At that time the minister did not know that the British government was giving consideration to the matter. Since then it has become obvious, through letters received by a number of members, and from comments in the press, that a large number of Canadian citizens are affected by the devaluation of the pound, and many people are taking an interest in it. Not only are those who are affected showing an interest, but it is obvious from press comments that a large number of their fellow Canadians are aware of the difficult circumstances faced by some people who have to exist in Canada today on imperial pensions.
Two general proposals have been made, the first being that the government should bring the plight of these people to the attention of the British government, explaining particularly the present circumstances, and the second, suggested by some veterans organizations, that the Canadian government should subsidize these imperial pensioners.
I am not going to discuss the soundness of this proposal, but I urge upon the minister that action be taken by the government at the earliest possible moment to bring to the attention of the British government the plight of certain imperial pensioners in Canada brought about by the recent devaluation of the nound.

Mr. Chairman, will the government move at this session to set up a special committee of the house on atomic energy? This suggestion has been made in different sessions, and I would point out to the ministry, particularly to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that the subject is now of even greater importance than it was in earlier years.
Only this morning we read in the press that yesterday in the United States the atomic

energy commission held a joint meeting with a committee of congress. The announcement from that meeting was made by the chairman of the committee of congress. The same United States congressional committee sent two representatives to Canada only a few weeks ago to inspect our plant at Chalk River.
It seems to me perfectly clear that the house should set up a committee on atomic energy. This request has been supported in other years, not only by members of the official opposition but also by the leaders of the C.C.F. and Social Credit parties. I am sure they will support my suggestion today. This is now one of the most important questions to be faced by our nation and by the House of Commons. I would urge that the government move to set up such a special committee without further delay.

May I confirm what has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, namely, that we have supported this suggestion in the past, and that we are happy to do so again today. This matter is one with which the House of Commons should be concerned. I do not suggest, of course, that any highly secret information should be imparted to such a committee, but I believe the house and country should know what Canada is doing in connection with the development and use of atomic energy.
In supporting a similar suggestion in past years I made the comment that this great scientific discovery could not be kept secret for any considerable length of time. The other afternoon the Prime Minister made the announcement that it was believed that the Soviet union had unlocked the secret of the atomic bomb. That had been anticipated by scientists, I believe, ever since the first bomb was dropped on Hiroshima in 1945,
In view of the necessity of having public opinion behind the government in its desire, as stated on more than one occasion before the United Nations, to bring atomic energy in all its phases under international control, I believe the time has now come when a committee should be established in order that parliament may be well informed and, in turn, in order that the people may have that information. Consequently I join with the hon. member in suggesting to the government that, in spite of all that has happened in the past, in view of the circumstances now surrounding this important discovery, and the dangers to the world flowing from it, if improperly used-and, on the other hand, the great benefits that might accrue to mankind if it is used properly and for the benefit of the human race-this house should know more about what Canada is doing, and the extent to which we are co-operating and have
Interim Supply
been permitted to co-operate with the United States, if I may put it that way. With reservations respecting highly secret matters, information should be given the house and the country on this important matter. In our opinion a committee on atomic matters should be set up by this house.	[DOT]

Mr. Chairman, I should like to indicate my support of the request by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra that a committee on atomic energy be set up at the earliest possible time. May I ask that the government give this matter its most earnest consideration at an early day.

I should like to support the suggestion just offered by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. I am sure hon. members could be most useful to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in connection with this matter of atomic energy. The entire administration of our share of what is being done in the matter of atomic energy is a heavy responsibility for one man to carry. I feel sure that hon. members could be helpful to him, particularly in the matter of exploration for atomic minerals.
The government has established a price of $2.75 a pound for uranium oxide. It would be interesting to know if that price is sufficiently high, and to know the quantities being exported. I suggest that if the minister can see his way clear he permit the setting up of this committee, because I believe it would be most helpful to him.

Perhaps I can shorten the debate. At the last session of the last parliament I stated that the government would have no objection to a committee on atomic energy. The government is still of the same opinion, and will be glad to co-operate with other parties in the house in the setting up of a committee at the proper time during this session.

I appreciate what the minister has just said. I hope this matter will be followed up and a committee set up at an early date.
I should like to broaden this discussion by urging upon the Prime Minister and the government the necessity for recasting the committee machinery of this house. The rules provide for about fifteen standing committees, which presumably will be appointed next week. Some of those committees will not meet for the duration of this session, while others will. The fact is that some committees have not met for years.
There are great areas of the public business that do not fall within the scope of any of the present standing committees. One has been mentioned this afternoon, this new sub-

Interim Supply
ject of atomic energy. There is another field that is completely omitted from the scope of the present standing committees, something of which I have spoken before. I refer to the whole subject of social security, welfare, health and housing, which I think should be embraced within the scope of a committee. When the government is giving consideration to amending or revising the present committee structure I hope we shall not be satisfied with a mere partial job. I submit that the time has come when someone must take the responsibility for going over the whole committee structure and recasting and modernizing it. If necessary, certain committees might be eliminated, because we do not wish to have too many. The duties of certain committees might be enlarged, but there should be committees to cover those fields of public business which are not covered at the present time. I urge again most strongly that provision be made in our committee structure for a committee on social security, welfare, health and housing.

Before we vote these several million dollars I should like to ask the minister a question. I had placed a question on the order paper which was answered today by the Minister of National Revenue, although only in part. My question was:
Are ambulance services considered to be part of medical expenses for the purposes of income tax and, if not, in what way does the government consider them not to be?
The answer given by the minister was as follows:
Amounts paid for ambulance services are not included in the medical expenses set forth in subsection (b) of section 26 of the Income Tax Act.
The last part of my question, which was not answered, reads as follows:
If not, in what way does the government consider them not to be?
The fact that that last part of the question was not answered would imply that the government have no answer to it. I do not believe they have. If a man becomes ill and has to call for an ambulance, that is certainly part of his medical expenses. The particular case that was drawn to my attention was that of a man who had to call an ambulance to take him two hundred miles. The expense was considerable, yet he could not include that as part of his medical expenses in making out his income tax return.
I appreciate the fact that there is a difference between the duties of the Minister of Finance and those of the Minister of National Revenue. The one imposes the taxes; the other collects them. The Minister of Finance hits the taxpayer on the head; the Minister of National Revenue drags him out. Some

of our citizens have to be dragged out anyway. I am going to ask the minister if he would care to express himself on this matter. He is asking for a lot of money which will have to come out of the taxpayer's pocket. I am quite sure we are willing to vote it, but it seems to me that consideration should be given to this particular phase of the Income Tax Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be glad to bring my hon. friend's question to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue. The position is that the act specifies-I have not the act before me-that medical expenses are deductible for income tax purposes. What constitutes medical expenses is a question for the Minister of National Revenue or his officials to determine. If the taxpayer is not satisfied, he can go to the courts for relief. I think that is as far as I can go in answering my hon. friend's question.
If the doctor included the charge for the ambulance in his bill, that could be deducted, could it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not the Minister of National Revenue; nor do I want to give free legal advice.
I understand that where a physician administers insulin or penicillin and includes the costs of the drugs in his bill, that expense can be deducted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For what it may be worth, my understanding is that if the cost of the medicines is included in the doctor's bill, they can be deducted, and if a hospital charged for the ambulance in its bill, it could be deducted. However, I do not think that that should be taken as a firm ruling. It is a matter for the administrative branch of the department to determine. If the taxpayer is dissatisfied, a remedy is provided in the act by way of appeal.

The trouble with the act is that there are different taxing officers across the country. A man in one section will give one ruling, and a man in another will give an entirely different ruling.
While I am on my feet I should like to bring something to the attention of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, who unfortunately is not in the house. There are thousands of people across Canada who are either renting or buying houses from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. These people are greatly inconvenienced by the fact that the offices of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are closed all day Saturday, although they are open from nine to five o'clock on week days. Many of the men who are renting or buying houses are working

from early morning until five or after five o'clock at night, and the only time they could go to the office would be at noon hour, at which time the officers of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are home eating their own lunches. I suggest that their offices be kept open on Saturday morning, or at least every other Saturday, so that the man of the house can go there to transact his business instead of his wife having to do it. I have had many letters about this from my own riding and other parts of Canada. It is something that should be seriously considered.

There is a matter of extreme urgency which I think it is my duty to place before the government. I refer to the charges being made for medical services and hospitalization provided for the Indians in the Rocky Mountain House section of Alberta. I say this is a matter of urgency, because tomorrow is the deadline so far as the medical men and the hospital authorities of Rocky Mountain House are concerned. Since 1948 the medical and hospital authorities at Rocky Mountain House in Alberta have been at loggerheads with the Indian affairs branch in connection with medical and hospital services for Indians. In the past it has been the policy of the medical men of the town of Rocky Mountain House to charge the minimum amounts set by the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons in connection with the various cases coming to their attention. Often the medical men have treated and hospitalized these Indians while having to postpone treatment of many of their regular patients because of lack of time and lack of hospital space.
These doctors have been submitting their bills to the Indian affairs branch at the minimum rates, and in almost every case those bills have been arbitrarily cut down by twenty to fifty per cent before being paid. The doctors urge that one of two things be done: either that they be paid a flat rate of $100 a month for treating the Indians-which incidentally was the amount recommended by the Alberta representative of the department-or that they work on the basis of the minimum rates established by the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons.
Ten months have elapsed since they began negotiations with the department. So far nothing has been done to reach any sort of agreement. Now the doctors have served notice that as and from tomorrow they will refuse to attend the Indians at less than the regular rates charged all other patients. This has become a very serious matter. Health conditions among the Indians in that area have not been good. The net result of what
Interim Supply
will happen after tomorrow, unless the department takes much-needed action, will be that the Indians will not receive this most essential service. The result will be deterioration not only of their own health, but also of the health of the white persons among whom these Indians move.
I know the Minister of Mines and Resources is not here today, but I urge that some other member of the government bring this matter to his attention. There is great urgency. Something must be done by tomorrow.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words to the Minister of Finance about an item in his own estimates, namely that relating to the wartime prices and trade board. The minister may say this is a matter we can discuss more fully when we reach that item, but that may not be for some weeks yet; and the March 31, 1950, deadline is also drawing near. It seems to me, therefore, that a few facts should be drawn to the attention of the minister at this time.
As he knows, the step he was forced to take a few days ago in devaluing the Canadian dollar could result in upward pressure being exerted on the cost of living in this country. In fact many people feel that this is happening already, that the pressure to increase the cost of living is greater than the pressure coming from the devaluation of the pound which might have served to bring down that cost.
This whole question of the high cost of living was highlighted a few days ago by a publication prepared by the welfare council of greater Toronto, entitled "A guide to family spending in Toronto, Canada, 1949." Hon. members probably saw in the Globe and Mail of Monday, September 26, a good summary of the findings contained in that report, but I would recommend that in addition they write the welfare council of greater Toronto and send fifty cents for a copy of the report, in which an excellent job has been done. The report makes it clear that, for ordinary decent living at today's prices, in the city of Toronto a family of five must have $50 a week.
I have some other figures as well. I am referring now to the Labour Gazette for July, 1949, in which I find on page 920 a table showing the hours and earnings by industries in Canada up to as late as April of this year. According to this table the average weekly wage in the manufacturing industries reporting to the dominion bureau of statistics was only $42.08 in April of this year. That table includes some industries in which the workers would earn more than this average, but it also includes figures such as these: $30.86 a week for those working in leather products; $29.41 a week for those engaged in making garments and personal furnishings. Then as I go away

Interim, Supply
down I find that the average weekly wage in highway construction was $33.92, while the average for those working in hotels and restaurants was $26.99. In this long column some are higher than the average of $42.08, but, as I have indicated, there are a great many away below that figure.
I think we in this House of Commons, who are fairly well fed-and who were given some very good apples today-must face the fact that it is exceedingly difficult for a great many Canadians to make both ends meet. If we put these figures side by side, those of the welfare council of greater Toronto showing that at today's prices a family of five must have $50 a week, and those of the Labour Gazette showing that there are thousands of people earning only $30, $35 and $40 a week, we can see that this is a very real problem.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister now, because we all know what government policy as to price control has been since the end of the war. We know where the legislation stands in regard to the wartime prices and trade board; unless something is brought in the whole set-up will vanish on March 31, 1950. For my part I should like to point out to the minister that he should start right now to do something to prevent the cost of living from going higher-indeed, to try to bring it down; but I know his view, and I know how long I would have to argue with him on that point. But I am going to appeal to him-and I hope he will consider this favourably-to have the administration of the wartime prices and trade board examined to see if he has a set-up there, with sufficient staff, which could do something about this job if even in his view -as it is in my view right now-it should become a problem demanding attention.
A moment ago I made reference to the devaluation of the dollar, and in that reference I admitted that it was a step the minister was forced to take. There are conditions in the world today that can have the effect of still further increasing the cost of living in this country; and bearing in mind what we have so often said from this corner of the house as to the excellent job in the field of price control done by the government during the war, it seems to me just as important to try to help the people of this country make both ends meet in time of peace. By the time we reach the appropriate item in the estimates, nothing may be left of the wartime prices and trade board. Certainly unless the government makes up its mind to do something about it before March 31, 1950, that organization will disappear. I urge upon the government, therefore, the importance of this whole question of keeping down the cost of

living, and I point out that it is something for which the government is responsible to the Canadian people.

I should like to take advantage of this opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to direct the attention of the house, and particularly the Minister of Veterans Affairs, to a matter I referred to in a speech delivered on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It is recorded in Hansard of September 21, page 141. In it there is a reference to what 1 consider to be one of these silly regulations affecting veterans who are attending our universities.
Last year, at the university of Toronto, eighty-three of these young veterans took second class honours in their final year. Of the eighty-three there were fifteen whose credits expired while they were writing the examinations after they had finished their academic year. Because of that regulation, those fifteen were deprived of the advantage of another year at the university on funds provided by the department. I suggest, as I did on a previous occasion, that the men who framed those regulations, as well as the minister, are just as anxious as I am to see that each of these veterans has an opportunity to complete his education.
As the minister knows, these boys left high school with their education half completed. Some of them left the university and gave to this country the best educational years of their lives. After years away from school they have returned to us to begin where they left off. It is unfair that, because of a regulation which must be applied mechanically, deserving young veterans who have shown that they have the ability and the desire to continue their education should be deprived of it. I suggest to the minister that that regulation be modified to this extent: that the student's academic year end not when he writes his last examination, but when he writes his first. I would urge upon the minister that he take this into consideration.
There is one other change I believe should be made. There should be a small committee -including the minister, if you like, and the senior officers who have charge of education in his department, and possibly someone from the university-charged with the responsibility of reviewing specific cases in which ability has been shown but the student is deprived of assistance because of this regulation. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that these regulations may be applied hard and fast in the mechanical field, but where human beings are concerned there should be some sort of committee or referee with discretionary powers.
I shall cite one example. A year ago a student graduated in the arts course in the

university of Toronto with an aggregate of approximately 800 marks on his final examinations. He was only two marks short of second-class honours. Because he was two marks short in an aggregate of 800, that student was deprived of any assistance during his post-graduate year at the college of education. He finally left college over $1,000 in debt because he had failed to secure another two marks. I marked examination papers for the department of education of Ontario for nearly twenty years. During his career I am sure the minister has marked enough examination papers to know that when you try to ascertain the difference in ability between a student who has 64 marks and one who has 66 marks, it is rather difficult. The marks received are largely determined by the attitude of the examiner at the time he marks the papers.
In cases of this kind I feel that these boys should be entitled to an appeal to some small committee with discretionary power to deal with the matter. I know the argument that will be raised against making any change in the regulations at this time. It is that some of those students who graduated during the past two or three years may want to take advantage of any change. I doubt whether many of them will. Most of those boys have secured jobs and are not likely to want to go back to the university. But suppose they do; suppose, as a result of this change, fifteen or twenty-five young veterans decide to return to university for post-graduate work. I would say, Mr. Chairman, and I am sure the minister is in agreement with me, that is in the best interests of this country. I am quite sure such a change would not be opposed on that ground. I realize that the minister cannot reply now, but I would ask him to give the matter his serious consideration.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, September 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Maurice Boisvert for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It is my pleasure, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate you upon your elevation to the chair. You were fully qualified for that high office because of your legal training, legal experience, and the fairness that you have shown in this house while you were the deputy speaker, and have shown since you have become the first commoner. I was particularly pleased to listen to you when you spoke in French. I note that you are a bilingual Speaker, a fact which is a great credit to you. I am sure that all members will appreciate your fairness and will feel that when you are in the chair they are safe in saying anything, within the rules.
It is also my great pleasure to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply. I have known the mover of the address for a long time. He is one of the brilliant members of the Quebec bar and has attained pre-eminence before the courts. He acquitted himself well. The seconder also spoke ably, and both of them deserve congratulations. As one of the senior members of this house, I am pleased to see all the good faces of the members who have been returned again and of those who have been elected here for the first time. The House of Commons is a gentlemen's club, and the new members should realize that the senior members will miss no opportunity to help them, whenever the occasion arises, so that they will fulfil their duties in the most pleasant atmosphere.
The last election was well run and it was very successful. If the Liberal party achieved such success, it is due in the first place to the personal campaign of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who crossed the country from Newfoundland to Victoria, addressing countless audiences, mixing with the people and shaking hands with countless friends. He did wonderfully well. I was not accustomed to that, but I remember that on one occasion, a year before his death, Mr. Lapointe had to conduct a campaign person-


ally. It was in the winter and he had to go across the country to preach the Liberal gospel. He did that successfully, but as a rule the people of Canada did not have the advantage of meeting the Prime Minister and the leader of the Liberal party personally. They had that privilege this year. What is to be admired in the Prime Minister is that he spoke the same language from coast to coast. Not only that, but he spoke without fear or favour. He spoke as a good Canadian. His language before English-speaking audiences was exactly the same as what he used in the province of Quebec: one language, one policy. The same things were said before audiences who spoke various languages. He was accompanied by his gracious wife, who also took pleasure in visiting all the constituencies of this country. The success of the election was to a large extent their personal reward. They took lots of trouble in campaigning all over the country and they were rewarded with the confidence of the people, who voted for the government after having heard the Prime Minister and after having met him and his wife.
In the elections previous to the last the general tenor of the speeches delivered by the Liberal speakers was that the other parties were worse than the Liberal party. This time the language used by Liberal speakers on the platform was entirely different. They did not say that other parties were worse than the Liberal party. They said that the Liberal party was better than opposition parties, and that it was the only party that could restore order in this country and bring welfare and prosperity from coast to coast-a great difference. It was of great importance and a great satisfaction to the Liberals who were denouncing only occasionally the Tories and the policies of the socialists and the Social Credit party. We told them what was going to be done for Canada by the Liberal party, for the welfare of Canada, for the future of our children, and the people liked it. They liked it so much that a tremendous number of people, who formerly were inclined to vote Conservative, socialist or Social Credit, decided to vote for the Liberal government headed by the present Prime Minister. They had real satisfaction when they voted. They knew that they were voting for a party that would fulfil its promises to them. If one travels anywhere in this country and says that he is a Liberal member of parliament he will be sure to have a good reception. That is why, sir, nobody should worry about the result of the eight by-elections which will take place next month. It is evident that the hurricane which has blown from Newfoundland to British Columbia inclusive will still carry the seats in the by-elections.

I have read the speech from the throne very carefully. There are many things in it, and most of them good. For instance, it is said that appeals to the privy council will be abolished-a very good thing. There are many other matters that I will not enumerate for the moment, but there is one of importance to which I draw the kind attention of the government and of all my fellow members. It is the amendment of the constitution. How can the parliament of Canada amend an imperial statute? Is it possible for the British parliament to delegate its power and authority to any other legislature in the commonwealth to amend its own statutes? I do not see how it could be done. Can we imagine that this parliament may amend any statute of the imperial parliament? It could not be done unless we made the statute of the imperial parliament, the British North America Act, our own by adopting exactly the same statute. If we did that, we might be able to amend the British North America Act after it had become an act of the parliament of Canada. But that would be very dangerous, and it would not work, because, when moving the second reading of the British North America Act in the House of Lords in 1867, Lord Carnarvon said:
To those resolutions-
He was referring to the Quebec resolutions. -all the British provinces in North America, were, as I have said, consenting parties and the measure founded upon them must be accepted as a treaty of union.
That was the language of Lord Carnarvon, who was then Secretary of State for the Colonies in the British government.
He spoke also of the appointment of a governor general. The present incumbent is one of the great men of the world, and so long as he occupies his office with dignity that is outstanding I do not see how we can make a suggestion for the appointment of anyone else. We should wait until his term of office is about to expire before we suggest the appointment of anyone else. However, that is not in the speech from the throne. All I have to say for the time being is that we are privileged to have as our governor general a man such as Lord Alexander, who is not only a distinguished soldier but also a great man.
I hold in my hand the text of the speech delivered at Westminster by Lord Carnarvon, where he went on to say:
Whilst the provisions regulating the constitution of the central parliament are in the nature of permanent enactments, those which govern the local legislatures will be subject to amendment by those bodies.
This deals with the question of amending the constitution. The provinces have the 45781-23
The Address-Mr. Pouliot right to amend their own constitutions, and Ottawa has not. That is quite strange. On the other hand, the legislation passed by the legislatures can be disallowed by this parliament, and the enactment of this parliament can be disallowed by the British government. That, too, is strange. How can we call Canada a sovereign nation so long as our laws are disallowed or may be disallowed by the British government? When His Majesty came here in 1939, and in the Senate chamber sanctioned some legislation, even those acts His Majesty had personally sanctioned were subject to disallowance by the British government within a period of two years.
So long as those provisions remain in the British North America Act can we call ourselves a free and sovereign nation? That cannot be. Let me read further from the words of Lord Carnarvon:
My lords, I now pass to that which is perhaps the most delicate and the most important part of this measure-the distribution of powers between the central parliament and the local authorities. In this is, I think, comprised the main theory and constitution of federal government; on this depends the practical working of the new system. And here we navigate a sea of difficulties. There are rocks on the right hand and on the left. If, on the one hand, the central government be too strong, then there is risk that it may absorb some of that local action, and that wholesome self-government by the provincial bodies, which it is a matter both of good faith and political expediency to maintain; if on the other hand, the central government is not strong enough, then arises a conflict of state rights and pretensions, cohesion is destroyed, and the effective vigour of the central authority is encroached upon. The real object which we have in view is to give the central government those high functions and almost sovereign powers by which general principles and uniformity of legislation may be secured in those questions that are of common import to all the provinces; and, at the same time, to retain for each province so ample a measure of municipal liberty and self-government as will allow and indeed compel them to exercise those local powers which they can exercise with great advantage to the community.
Then he goes on to say:
As I have said, it is proposed that the provinces shall surrender to the central parliament all powers of raising revenue, except by direct taxation. In return for this concession the central government will remit to the local legislatures certain fixed sums and proportionate capitation payments, in order to enable them more conveniently to defray the costs of local administration.
This happened at the time of confederation, and the amounts are mentioned in the British North America Act. Lord Carnarvon continues:
A legislative union is, under existing circumstances, impracticable.
I would suggest that my fellow colleagues read this speech by the then secretary for the colonies. I am sure they would find it illuminating, because it expresses the law-

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
makers' intent with respect to our constitution.
To summarize, it would be most delicate and dangerous to amend the constitution at the present time, because it was precisely drafted in such a way that it could not be amended. This is the source of the difficulties encountered by those who have thought of amending the constitution and who have not yet found a way to do it. We shall not ignore the fact that the imperial parliament and the Canadian parliament are two different bodies; and at the present time, owing to the fact that the constitution of Canada is an act of the imperial parliament, we have to go to them for any amendment requested by this country.
I should be greatly surprised if the British parliament surrendered to Canada the right to amend imperial legislation. It could be done in only one way, namely if the amendment were first granted by the British parliament. One or two amendments could be made at a time, the amendment having been passed first by the British parliament and then our having been given permission to repeat a similar procedure. We would on the second occasion do that which would have been done in the first place by the British parliament. If the British parliament did not first make the amendment, then I do not see how we could make it.
Therefore this presents a most difficult problem. It is not difficult from the legislative point of view but, as Lord Carnarvon has said, this constitution is a sort of treaty of union. This means that the consent of all interested parties should be called for; and I do not see how under such conditions anyone would surrender any right and give a blank cheque.
I urge the government to be careful in amending the constitution. Many people have referred to this as being an indication of progress, and it may be or not. I shall never say that the constitution does not need to be amended as there is much deadwood in the British North America Act after 82 years, but the manner of dealing with the respective jurisdictions should be thought over for a long time in order that the best possible results may be obtained. That is why it is not without a certain amount of concern that I have noticed that a change may be made in the respective and exclusive jurisdictions now provided by the British North America Act.
I do not say that it cannot be done, but it should be done with the utmost care in order to respect the rights of all those who were parties to the first "treaty of union", which is Lord Carnarvon's expression. I am not an imperialist, far from it, nor am I an
IMr. Pouliot.]
isolationist; I am a Canadian. I think that all those who have been born in this country and all those who have made Canada their true country of adoption should think of the future and should put sentiment aside in order to find the best way to govern this country.
There is some colonialism still prevailing in some parts of this country. What is colonialism? An hon. member across the floor asked that question yesterday. Colonialism is simply an inferiority complex with regard to the seat of the empire, something that exists in the minds of some who do not live in the United Kingdom. An Englishman who lives or is domiciled in the United Kingdom has the right to be an imperialist; it is natural that he would want his country to be extended as far as possible; but for one who claims he is a Canadian, for one who is domiciled in Canada, to be an imperialist is sheer nonsense.
There are some hon. members who are still imbued with the spirit of colonialism; they still live in the darkness of ignorance, in the shade of the tree of death like the barbarians of olden times. I have quoted a great English statesman to that effect. How can anyone in Canada claim that he is an imperialist and a good Canadian at the same time? That is impossible. It is like trying to square the circle, which is an absurdity. I do not say that because I have no English friends; I simply regret that some who should be proud of their country have a feeling of colonialism in the year 1949.
Because a vast majority of Canadian people did not have that feeling of colonialism, for the first time in many years a leader of a great party was applauded throughout the land because he extolled the virtues and merits of pure Canadianism. The reason I am so happy to give my full support to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is that while he is the head of the government he is no despot. He takes hon. members into his confidence. He consults the members of parliament on every important issue and stands by them. It is only natural that hon. members stand by him and by the members of his cabinet.
My great grandfather voted for the resolution before the Act of Union. My grandfather voted for Blake and Alexander Mackenzie. My father was elected with Laurier in 1896. I am proud to support the Liberal government that we now have in this House of Commons.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words shall be of personal congratulation to the gentleman who has been named Speaker of this house. There seems to be a spirit of unanimity in at least that one thing.

I think almost everyone is agreed that the government should be congratulated upon its choice. Congratulations seem to be in order this session, congratulations to the new government, to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), to the mover (Mr. Boisvert) and the seconder (Mr. Laing) of the address, to the new appointees, to new members of the house generally, and perhaps in particular to the new members from that new province, the name of which has been so consistently and variously mispronounced.
I wonder if the hon. members from that new province of Newfoundland are all orators? I was greatly delighted with their first speeches, particularly with the speech of a gentleman who has become my friend, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins). I envy him the purity of his language, the clarity of his enunciation, and his deep knowledge of the subject about which he spoke. May I at the outset join with other hon. members in their congratulations to all these gentlemen.
Perhaps I should reserve special congratulations for two of the new and younger members on the government side. May I say at once that I am sorry they were elected, because they replace two colleagues of my own party, two friends of mine who were formerly in this house. But since in a democracy the electors must be the final arbiters, and since these gentlemen have been elected, I wish them every success. I refer to the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson), whom I see not in his own but in someone else's seat, and the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison), young men who for a short time were my pupils. Since the indoctrination of political views is not one of the functions of a teacher, I accept no responsibility for the error of their ways in matters political. Nevertheless, to me their success must be a matter of some personal gratification, for indeed already they may be said to have achieved success since they have been deemed worthy by their fellow men to represent them in this honourable house.
There seems to be an air of peace and quietness about the house this session to which we were not accustomed last session. I think that may be a change for the good. After the battle comes peace, at least temporarily. I believe I have observed a change in the attitude of certain of my hon. friends which may augur well for the speedy conduct of government business this session. The victory of the Liberal party at the polls was clear and decisive. No one has tried to deny that. It is to be hoped that the very greatness of that victory may not work against good government, that it may not result in an apathy bred of the consciousness 45781-231
The Address-Mr. Knight of power. The power of this government is indeed great; and just as noblesse oblige, so has greatness its obligations. No longer can this government plead a narrow majority as an excuse for inaction in connection with the things the country needs. I hope we shall not have an example of one-party government in this country. This house has an overwhelming majority of Liberal members, though I should point out that they represent only 49-54 per cent of the voters of this country, according to the information contained in a handy little book published by the Canadian Press containing the results of the recent election. According to that same source, there must be in the province of Quebec 600,000 voters-and that figure is conservative

who voted against the policies of the government, but they are represented in this house by only five members, two Progressive Conservatives and three Independents. To me that is an unfortunate situation; the representation of those people certainly is not adequate.
So much for the House of Commons. When we turn to the Senate we find that it has 102 members, of whom all but 15 were appointed by a Liberal government. While I do not grant that other place sufficient importance to become a danger, nevertheless its membership, considered from the point of view of political representation, is extremely disproportionate to the population of the country. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) the other day went so far as to suggest that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) might very well appoint to that body a gentleman who belongs to an opposition political party, mentioning him by name. I shall not go that far, but I would go sc far as to suggest to the Prime Minister that he might be sufficiently magnanimous to appoint, irrespective of their political views, men and women who deserve well of their country and who have served in spheres of life other than political, perhaps people prominent in business, agriculture, labour, professional life, literature or art. If the representation of the parties in the upper house were anywhere near equal, that might be too much to ask; but with the present enormous Liberal majority I think it is a reasonable request.
I have spoken of the House of Commons and of the other place. There remains the judiciary. In our province it is common talk that to become a judge one must first of all be a lawyer, next a Liberal, and third either a defeated candidate who ran in the interests of the Liberal party or at least a member and preferably the chairman of a Liberal party executive. An examination of appointments
35S

The Address-Mr. Knight in that province, both recent and otherwise, might throw some light on that point, though I have not the information before me at the moment. Then there are the civil servants throughout the country. I do not know how they are appointed, but if the recommendations of members of parliament are taken into account I would suggest that probably those appointments are heavily loaded, with the balance on the Liberal side.
This whole situation, as I see it, constitutes a danger not only to this country but to the government which is in charge of our affairs. They have indeed great power. Let them see to it that their power is not abused. As a member of this party, smaller indeed since the recent election, for reasons I shall not broach here, may I say that we shall continue to act as the conscience of this government. We shall continue to create in the public mind a demand for those reforms and changes needed by the people of this country, and shall continue to press upon the government the need to put those reforms and changes into effect.
Legislation to effect one of those changes is now before the house, and here I touch upon the matter which was the subject of the speech by my hon. and genial friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). At last we have reached the point where we are ready to show our maturity as a nation and take that final step, which we have not taken sooner for no other reason than timidity, perhaps natural in a nation making its independent debut in international affairs; one might say as a fledgling long nurtured and protected under its mother's wing. The abolition of appeals to the privy council is but a symbol of something which has long been an actual fact: that we are a great and independent nation. We can shake off that dependency perhaps more easily than we can shake off the inferiority complex of which the hon. member has spoken, a complex which has been engendered by that dependency, which carries over from the field of external affairs into other spheres. While we have a culture which is unique and worthy of perpetuation and preservation, we have been content to imitate. Particularly in the spheres of art and literature, I think, we have scoured foreign fields while neglecting the beauty and inspiration of our own. Consciousness of a new nationhood, it is to be hoped, will awaken us to a sufficient pride in the unique and piquant flavour of our own culture to ensure that we do not allow it to be watered down to a tasteless and insipid uniformity. To this end, we need certain conditions. I would say that the first condition we need is the assurance of a long period of peace. Living temporarily


upon the crater of an extinct volcano is not conducive to the production of creative art. It is when the mind is free from fear and the body is free from want that men's minds turn to those things which lift mere existence into the realm of worth-while living.
Peace is the greatest need of the world today. We have been apt to assess our progress in terms of ability to produce gadgets, but our application of our inventive genius in the field of science may destroy us all, nay, will destroy us unless we can accompany it with the development of a moral sense. The material assets of which we are so proud could be wiped out overnight by any maniac with an atomic bomb. Even more potent instruments of mass death and destruction are now in existence.
We need peace and we need enlightenment. We need education. When I speak of education I am not thinking of some quick training, some technical course or some vocational training to enable one to earn a living, some intensive course in physics or ballistics which enables a young man to operate a machine gun or an aeroplane. I am thinking of education as a thing of the mind and spirit, a development of the personality, an appreciation of the finer things in life, the development of sound judgment and the ability to analyse things. Were we, as a nation, in possession of these qualities then there might be some justification for our cheek in boasting about our way of life and suggesting that other countries might well adopt it.
This government at Ottawa has some responsibility in this matter. I was pleased when the Prime Minister recognized that fact in the session earlier this year, and announced the appointment of a royal commission on cultural matters. I am glad such a commission is now operating. For some years I tried to persuade the Prime Minister, in his capacity as Secretary of State for External Affairs, to set up in Canada a commission of the United Nations educational, scientific and cultural organization. He categorically refused to accede to my request. However, what's in a name? The important thing is that something is now being done. We hope that whatever advice is given to the government by that commission, it will be followed by the appropriate action. I remember that during- the debate in the last session the Prime Minister promised, and it is recorded in Hansard, that this would not be just a hope commission, but a commission of action.
During the recent election campaign, the Prime Minister was reported as stating that Canadian universities should be supported in their work, or at least that it would be a pity if their work were to fall off owing to lack
35?

of support. I believe the dominion government must accept some responsibility for the rather backward state of education in some sections of our country because it has persistently refused to aid the provinces in this connection. The universities are short of funds. Great numbers of the veteran students are now graduating into the life of our nation, having been rehabilitated through education provided by D.V.A. At this moment [ should like to congratulate the government on the success of that scheme. As I said, some universities are financially embarrassed, and some schools are indeed the poor relations of others.
Taxation for educational purposes must be put upon a broader base than a levy on real property. In that direction lies inequality of opportunity. At a later date, I hope to discuss this whole question; but at this time I point out that the idea that federal aid should be extended to education is becoming more and more generally accepted. It has been discovered by those who during the war accepted federal aid for technical and vocational education, and those who participated in dominion-provincial schemes of assistance to certain worthy students, that federal aid by no means involves federal interference. Many who witnessed the great educational venture of the dominion government in the rehabilitation of war veterans through education have reconsidered this question. My own view is that the fear of federal interference in the administration of education was largely due to a feeling of inferiority which had developed, and not only in the direction mentioned by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot).
I believe the aid I advocate is one positive approach to the problem of preserving the unique qualities of our culture and the promotion of enlightenment which I have mentioned as a desirable thing; nay, which I think is fundamental. During the war, we subsidized this and put a floor under that, but we allowed education to become one of the first casualties.
In attempting to weed out of our national life those things which are detrimental to our ideals of culture there is, of course, the negative approach. In this, too, we have a responsibility. I do not wish to say anything against the culture of our friends to the south, but I would point out that we have in our own land something unique, something which is typically Canadian. It is my belief we should not make a practice of copying others but we should develop something of our own.
During the course of the summer, I stopped at a tourist camp in Canada and noticed the
The Address-Mr. Knight place was decorated with United States flags. I went to the lady who was in charge and asked the reason for the display of these flags. She said, "Well, sir, we want to make our American friends feel at home." I believe hon. members in this house will recognize the fallacy of that argument. What our United States friends wanted to feel was that they were in Canada, not at home. It was largely for that reason they came to visit us.
Our young people spend approximately five hours a day in educational institutions and the remainder of their waking hours in what we might call their ordinary environment, the home, the street, or the playing field. Surely, this parliament has an interest and responsibility in the quality of that environment. I note the increase in juvenile delinquency, the increase in the number of divorce cases, and I ponder over the fact that our penitentiaries are filled with young men.
Let us look at some of the negative agencies in this environment. High on the list comes the cheap vulgarity of many commercial radio programs, some moving pictures, the "slick" magazines, the so-called "comic" books, the red and yellow novels which flood the counters of our news stands.
That compels me to face the question of censorship. I am not sure that I favour the censorship of reading material, although it is a matter to which I have given some study. Such censorship as is exercised through the Department of National Revenue is, in my opinion, inefficient and ineffective. I admit that censorship is a tremendously difficult task; because of that fact competent people should be in charge of it. In an investigation which I made during the last session into the censorship of books, I made several startling discoveries. For example, I found that the men who had the final decision on the censorship of books were not fitted either by background, education, experience or training for the task they had to perform. Books denied entry at one customs port were being admitted at others. Entry was being denied books which in my opinion should have been admitted. Books were being allowed in which should have been kept out. I am referring, of course, to books written and published outside of this country. The censorship of foreign-language books is quite inefficient. I have a good deal of material on my files on that point but I shall not weary the house with it because it is not the main subject of my discussion today. I shall content myself by saying that the censorship of foreign-language books and domestic books was particularly inadequate. No great distinction seemed to be made between books which evidenced a necessary realism in the treatment of the subjects with which they

The Address-Mr. Knight dealt, and those which were purely and deliberately pornographic and were made filthy tor the sole purpose that they might become best sellers, with the resulting profit.
In this connection also there is the difficulty of protecting the young without restricting the liberties of the adult, the liberties of those whose character, such as it is, has already been formed. There is the difficulty of restricting the activities of some business people who will sell anything to anyone as long as there is money to be made, and unless there are definite protective laws against it.
The negative approach is admittedly difficult. The positive one is feasible, if inadequate. Tastes are formed through use. We must substitute the useful for the harmful, the good for the evil. In the matter of reading for young people, that procedure at the moment is difficult through lack of material. One does not travel far in other countries until one realizes that on this continent, and particularly in this country perhaps, there is a great dearth of suitable reading for boys and girls. We have for so long accepted the suggestion that the comic book is all that is necessary that we just say: Oh, he has the comics, hasn't he? For years we have accepted the suggestion that the comic book solves the problem. I would express the hope that perhaps with this new consciousness of nationhood, or this awakening of nationhood, we shall not so neglect our youth in the future.
I have, sir, made a plea for the preservation and encouragement of our Canadian culture as such. I have suggested that the government has some responsibility in that matter, and have put forward some suggestions as to how they might marshal that assistance. Finally, let me urge that we cast out this inferiority, that we cast out fear. Let us have confidence in ourselves and in our abilities. Let us beware of taking the shadow for the substance. Let us refuse the easy way, the temptation to adopt a juke-box civilization, all noise and glitter. Let us be originators, not imitators. In short, sir, let us be Canadians, strong in the faith that we too have something distinctive, something precious and unique, to contribute to the community of men.
We have a great country. We are the trustees of a great heritage. Let us keep alive the flame of Canadian culture. It may be dim at the moment but it may be brighter tomorrow. I am reminded of some words of John Buchan, a former governor general who, may I suggest in all humility, if he were to hear me today, would largely agree with what I have said. His words were these:
The spark, once transmitted, may smoulder for generations under ashes, but the appointed time will come, and it will flare up to warm the world.
