I should like first to congratulate you, sir, on your appointment as Deputy Speaker and through you to offer my congratulations to the Speaker on his election as first commoner. I am sure, as I know are all other members of this chamber, that you will both discharge your high and important functions with dignity and justice.
I should like to compliment the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and all of the other new members of this house who have so far taken part in this debate. Their speeches have been excellent and indicate that they all have something of importance to contribute to this house.
Today there are several matters on which I should like to make brief comment, the first of which is the revision of the Indian Act. This act has not had any main revision for something over fifty years. As a result, it is greatly out of date, a fact which makes it difficult for the officials of the Indian affairs branch to administer that department in the best way possible for the Indians of this country and in a way which is in conformity with the general advance in ideas that has taken place over that period of time. This fact was recognized, and in 1946 the following resolution was passed in this house:
That a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons be appointed to examine and consider the Indian Act, chapter 98, R.S.C., 1927, and amendments thereto and to suggest such amendments as they deem advisable, with authority to investigate and report upon Indian administration in general and, in particular, the following matters:
And the matters are listed. As a result of that resolution a committee was set up. This committee held long sessions throughout 1946, 1947 and 1948. It received evidence from several hundred witnesses. A great deal of work on the part of departmental officials was devoted to the committee and to the securing of information for it. As a result of the sittings of that committee a series of recommendations were made to this house. They were adopted, and as a result I think a considerable improvement took place in the administration of the Indian affairs branch. For one thing, a large number of day schools have been and are being built at the present time, to improve the educational facilities for our Indians.
Hospital and medical care have also improved considerably. However, the main purpose for which the committee was set up, namely, to amend the Indian Act, has not been carried to fruition. In spite of
OWr. Knight.]

the urgings of myself and a considerable number of hon. members at the last session of the last parliament, the government did not see fit to introduce the suggested amendments to the act which had been made in previous years. Only a day or two ago the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) asked the government whether they intended to introduce at this session legislation to amend the Indian Act. The answer of the minister, as reported at page 232 of Hansard, was as follows:
A draft bill to amend the Indian Act is in the hands of the Department of Justice, but I am not able to say when it will be available for consideration by the house.
That was the situation in 1948. After the committee had spent this long period in debating the suggested amendments to the act the thing was put into the hands of the Department of Justice, and apparently it has remained there ever since. Surely the officials of the Department of Justice have had time to look into the matter and have it ready for presentation to the house. I strongly urge upon the government that a revised Indian Act be introduced into the house just as rapidly as possible. If the government is still not satisfied with the draft bill that was prepared by the committee and revised by the Justice department, then I would ask that the joint committee be reconstituted just as quickly as that can be done, so that the work can be gone on with. The Indians of the country, and a large number of other people lyho are interested in their welfare, hoped for great things from the setting up of the committee on Indian affairs and the revision of the act. The government has a moral duty to have this matter brought to completion just as soon as it can possibly do so.
I should now like to say something about a matter which was brought up by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), this afternoon, and earlier this week by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), namely, the difficult situation in which imperial veterans now find themselves as the result of the devaluation of the British pound. I hold in my hand a resolution which was forwarded to me by the Calgary branch of the Army, Navy and Air Force Veterans Association, urging this action upon the government. The exact way in which this could be done I do not wish to suggest. One thing which would help considerably, as far as some of these men are concerned, is the extension of the war veterans allowance to them. Apart from that, some arrangement might be come to between this government and the British government in the matter of bringing these men's pensions back to the
The Address-Mr. Harkness level at which they were before the pound was devalued or when the pound was at the normal rate of exchange; or, as suggested in this resolution, this government might supplement the British pensions in order to bring them back up to what the normal rate would make them.
Another matter along that line which I should like to mention is the plight of the superannuated civil servants. I have had several pitiable letters from ex-dominion civil servants who have been superannuated on extremely small pensions. I should like to bring them to the attention of the government and request that something be done particularly for those men who have pensions smaller than the old age pension paid. Quite a number of these people, although they worked for many long years for the Dominion of Canada, have pensions considerably smaller than that to which they would be entitled if they were able to draw old age pensions. In most cases these men are in the age bracket of from 65 to 70. Since there has been a great deal of talk and, as I remember, quite a few promises by the government that the old age pension age would be brought down to 65, they could very well start to redeem these promises by giving to these superannuated civil servants allowances at least sufficiently large to bring them up to the scale of the old age pension.
So far in this debate we have heard considerable talk about irrigation. There is one phase of that matter that I should like to say something about. In western Canada we are beginning to use the sprinkler system of irrigation, in which a pump and a system of pipes, and so on, are used to put water on the land rather than levelling it off and putting it on by means of ditches. It possesses many advantages over the levelling and ditching system. It means that a great deal of land, which could not have been irrigated otherwise, can be brought under irrigation. One of the difficulties in connection with it is that the machinery needed-the pump, the pipes, and so forth-is subject to duty and tax. I know of two farmers in the area east of Calgary who, being desperate because of the drought conditions there in the past summer, imported this, machinery from the United States and they had to pay a tax of over $1,100. Their contention, which I think is perfectly justifiable, is that this type of equipment should be classed as farm machinery, and as such not subject to tariff and taxes. I would ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), who fortunately, I see, is sitting across from me, to bear this fact in mind when he is making up his budget resolutions. I may say that I took this matter up with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann)

The Address-Mr. Harkness and asked him whether it would be possible for his department to make a ruling that this type of machinery was indeed farm machinery, as it is, and thus not subject to duty and tax. His reply, however, was:
To permit of the duty free entry of such apparatus, a tariff change would be necessary. Amendments to the tariff do not come under my department, being rather the responsibility of the Department of Finance.
It seems to me this is a matter in which the Department of Finance could move immediately, and in doing so could bring aid in irrigation to considerable areas in western Canada where water is available and can be used by means of this sprinkler system.
I should now like to say something on the subject of defence. During past years we in the official opposition have made repeated efforts to secure information in regard to the state of the defences of this country. In many instances these efforts were far from successful. The information was denied to us. However, a general picture was always built up by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), both here and throughout the country at large, that our defence situation was excellent; that we had a small but mobile highly trained hard-hitting defence force, which was capable of dealing with any eventualities it was possible to foresee arising. It was well adapted to deal especially with the only thing that we could reasonably expect in this country, at the start of a war at any rate, namely, diversionary raids particularly on our northern airfields.
Well, during the past summer an exercise was held in the Peace river valley to test, apparently-at least that was what was given out in the newspapers-the ability of our defence forces to meet a diversionary raid of this nature. It was known as Exercise Eagle. The result has been rather unfortunate. The chief feature which strikes me in this connection is that the exercise showed a tragic lack of proper equipment on the part of our defence forces. This is the sort of thing which appeared in the newspapers all across this country-and I shall proceed to read a few extracts to show what these correspondents, most of whom were men who had seen service overseas, thought of the equipment of our defence forces.
The first of these is from the Vancouver Daily Province of August 8. This is an account by Ross Munro, stating-
The exercise clearly revealed some startling weaknesses in our defence picture.
The most alarming feature is the almost-complete inadequacy of the R.C.A.F. operational aircraft to meet attack. The combat planes are too old and too few.
Further on in the same article he speaks about the good performance put on by the
tMr. Harkness.]
P.P.C.L.I., an infantry regiment stationed at Calgary, which has now been trained as a parachutist regiment. Referring to that unit he says:
But even the P.F.C.L.I. need more equipment; for example, they had to borrow most of their parachutes from the joint air school at Rivers, Manitoba, for this scheme. They also borrowed 150 jump tunics.
And further on, referring to the aircraft used in the exercise, he states:
In regard to the types of planes, the most astonishing thing was that there wasn't a single jet fighter in the whole exercise.
They weren't put on "Eagle" because they had been worked hard during the two-week summer camp of the western reserve squadrons and maintenance problems were too tough for operating up here.
The most modern plane was the Mustang fighter and the R.C.A.F. even had to call on Rockcliffe and Trenton stations in Ontario to make up a nine-plane squadron.
But the bulk of the "fighters" were the old Harvard trainers. Then there were obsolete Mitchell bombers-six of them.
The majority of the pilots were civilian reserve officers and they showed they could do a job. But again they had so little to work with.
The air force staffs also executed their tasks of planning and directing extremely well.
The "tools" of war were lacking. The R.C.A.F. and exercise "Eagle" foundered on that point in its application to air force performance in an emergency at this time.
And here is an article by Paul St. Pierre which appeared in the Vancouver Sun of August 8:
Russia could play havoc in our northland today if she successfully launched an airborne .attack of sacrifice troops. H any Canadian officer disagrees with this he is not among the dozen with whom I spoke.
And later in the same article he says:
But it was a distressing sight to see a young, enthusiastic paratrooper trotting about the battle scene with an alder stick with a tin can nailed on top. "That's a trench mortar," an officer explained.
There were many other newspaper accounts along the same line. In one of them, I remember, there was a complaint that the heavy machine guns used by the P.P.C.L.I. in this exercise-or at least some of them-were not equipped with sights. They did not have the sights for them.
What all this leads us to is the fact that during the past three years we have voted large sums of money for the defence forces. We in the official opposition have tried to And out the purposes for which the money was being used, if it was being properly spent, and if we were getting the efficient and effective fighting force to which the expenditures entitle us. We were denied that information and told that everything was fine. When an exercise of this sort takes place we find everything is not fine.

The accounts sent out by the correspondents who were there indicate that the men were all right. The P.P.C.L.I. put up a magnificent performance. Fighter pilots and other air crew did excellent work. The staff work was all right. The thing that was wrong and which caused the exercise to fail was the fact that proper equipment was not there. We did not have it in this country.
We have maintained right along that a defence committee of the House of Commons should be set up to which full information could be given respecting the state of our defence forces. The situation brought to light by Exercise Eagle reinforces that contention, and points up strongly the fact that the house needs a committee of that kind which could get more information about defence.
It is our duty to see that the moneys voted for defence purposes are properly spent. From what we can make out, they may have been properly spent, and they may not. At any rate we have not got what we paid for. We have not an effective fighting force. In theory we are supposed to have an airborne [DOT] brigade which could stop any diversionary raid on this country. We are supposed to have an air force which would transport them to the place where they would be needed. This exercise demonstrated that we have not those things. We have not the equipment which would make it possible for our men to do the job.
In my view the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) should, in fact must, make a full explanation to the house as to exactly what did happen, what the situation was in this exercise, and just what the situation is at the present time, so far as defence preparations are concerned. In particular we should be told the situation from the standpoint of equipment, one feature in connection with which we appear to be especially weak.
There is one other phase of defence matters upon which I should like to touch briefly, namely passive defence measures against atomic warfare. I discussed this matter last February in the debate in reply to the speech from the throne, and at that time requested the minister to make a statement as to what passive defence measures this country had taken. I have not yet received an answer to that question.
I know that over a year ago the government appointed General Worthington, a most capable officer, to survey this situation. Whether his survey has been completed or not, or what he has recommended, has never been made public so far as I am aware. As for this country's being protected in the event of another war, I think perhaps it is
The Address-Mr. Harkness more necessary to take proper measures of passive defence than to do anything else, including the building up of our actual defence forces.
The news which came last week, that the Russians now apparently have atomic bombs, makes this more urgent. It brings the matter into sharp focus and makes it imperative that steps be taken to protect the civilian population in the event of war breaking out. That is not so very unlikely, although we hope, trust and pray that it will not take place. In my opinion there is no question that long before this we should have been taking a considerable number of measures to protect the general public in the event of the dropping of atomic bombs. These would be measures planning for the evacuation of people from our larger centres of population.
I suggested last February that in considering its housing plans and various schemes to aid the construction of houses the government should make it possible for those who wanted to build houses in the smaller centres to obtain the same assistance given to those who were building in the more densely populated areas. It would seem that a reverse policy has been adopted. From what I can make out it is much easier to obtain help under the National Housing Act for the building of houses in the larger centres of population than it is for the building of houses in the smaller centres.
At that time I pointed out, and I still am strongly of the same opinion, that efforts should be made through the industrial development bank to bring about a dispersion of industry which would carry with it a dispersion of population because people will go where they can get work.
I shall come back to both aspects of this matter of defence to which I have referred when the estimates are before us, but in the meantime I ask the minister to be prepared, either during this debate or when his estimates are before us, to make a full statement and answer the questions which have been posed here.

speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the people of my constituency would want me to pay a tribute to my predecessor, Mr. James A. Marshall, who has so ably represented Cam-rose in this house over thg past fourteen years. By keeping close contact with the people of the constituency he has won the esteem of all. It was with deep regret that they received his decision to resign.
I should also like to say a few words with regard to the wonderful agricultural constituency which I now have the honour to represent. In Camrose we have one of the finest mixed farming districts in Canada. We are proud to say that we have a greater number of registered seed growers than are to be found in any other part of Alberta. We cannot claim the honour of having the world's wheat king. He happens to live in the nearby constituency of Red Deer. We can, however, claim the honour of having the world's rye king. In addition, we have several other farmers who have won recognition in the field of agriculture. In the matter of purebred livestock, our herds are comparable to the best in Canada. In this field also it is not uncommon for one of our farmers to produce a champion.
In addition to a well-balanced mixed farming district we have several coal mines in the constituency. From those mines we export a considerable amount of coal each year. The oil industry in the Camrose constituency is as yet in its infancy. So far we have only one well; it is located at Stettler. We hope, however, that this is only the forerunner of a more prosperous field.
Generally speaking, the Camrose constituency is well blessed, but we have a few problems which I would bring to the attention of the government at this time. Those problems are not peculiar to this constituency alone. They would affect most other parts of Canada. In order to make a good agricultural district better we would suggest that the government should provide: rMr. Speaker.]

1.	Low cost credit facilities through agencies especially acquainted with agricultural and marketing conditions.
2.	Fair prices sufficient to cover the average production costs and to give primary producers a fair net return for their services based on parity.
3.	The Canadian wheat board should be revised so that the board becomes an agency operating primarily for the benefit of the producer.
4.	Stability of our basic industry through long-term international wheat agreements.
5.	Permanent agricultural prices support legislation.
6.	Producer representation on all boards and agencies having control over farm products.
If the government would consider these measures, it would tend to make farming, not only in our constituency but in the rest of Canada, much better for all concerned.
At this time I would also mention the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Farmers who have for many years been paying into this fund at the rate of one per cent on all grain sold suddenly find that in time of need they are unable to derive any benefit under the act simply because their farms happen to be on the wrong side of the township line. Surely there must be a more equitable manner in which this act could be administered. I understand that it is coming up for revision this session, and I would urge the government to consider this matter.
In our constituency, as in other parts of Canada, there are a number of senior citizens who are commonly known as old age pensioners. They were pleased to receive a $10 increase in their pension just before the last federal election. They would be more pleased, however, if the government could see fit also to raise the ceiling of their earning power. Many of our old age pensioners are bedridden. They are not considered to be bad enough to be hospitalized, but at the same time they are unable to care for themselves. In these cases the pension paid is not sufficient to take care of their needs. I think that is a matter which should be considered. Another nice gesture would be for the government to issue to each old age pensioner a radio licence which would be valid for the rest of his life.
I should also like to say a few words with regard to freight rates. Many rumours have been circulating with regard to a proposed increase in freight rates. At this moment I should like to say that the people of my constituency would be absolutely opposed to any change in the freight structure, especially the Crowsnest pass agreement, unless the change were in a downward direction.

Those are some of the problems which confront the people of my constituency. It might be argued that these proposals would take a considerable amount of financing. In reply,
I would refer to Hansard of Tuesday, March 22, 1949. On page 5 of the appendix to the budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will be found a chart. This chart shows the gross national income and the gross national product for a period of eleven years, beginning with 1938 and going up to 1948. The interesting thing about this chart is that in every year, as will be noticed, the column which represents the gross national production is always greater than the column representing the gross national income.
In other words, the flow of prices is always greater than the flow of purchasing power. That is to say, at any given time we are never able to buy back the goods of our producers. Carrying this argument a little bit further, I refer to the Canada Year Book. At page 1089 of the 1948-49 edition it will be found that the net national income in 1947 was $10,981 million and that the net national production in 1947 was $13,375 million. In other words, in that year there was a shortage of $2,394 million; we were that much short of being able to buy back our production.
We could trade some of that surplus with other nations to our mutual advantage, and if we did so we would still have the same amount left on our shelves. Therefore, taking 1947 as an example, we would have $2,394 million worth of goods lying on the shelves. These goods represent real wealth. I suggest that the government should create a commission, which would be responsible to the people through parliament, to take these goods on the shelves and use them as a backing for the creation of new credit, and in this way we would be able to finance the proposals I have outlined today.

Immediately following the war, the government spent a great deal of money providing emergency shelter for the returned veterans. Army barracks and anything else that would provide shelter were converted into temporary housing units. The wartime housing scheme has been extended to over 1,200 units. Much of the so-called temporary housing accommodation has become permanent because it has been occupied for four or five years now.
Before the war Edmonton was known for its wide open spaces. Today there is scarcely a lot that is undeveloped. The city has been forced to extend utilities to areas which were previously agricultural. The city has done a good job under difficult conditions. From two to three thousand houses have been built per year since the end of the war but this does not even keep up with the increase and certainly does not replace the temporary shelters. So far as housing is concerned, I would say Edmonton was at the explosive point.
I was pleased with the proposals made by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) last week. In the first place his proposals would reduce the down payment required which should make eventual home ownership possible for a large number of young people. There is also a proposal for federal government assistance to the provinces and municipalities in providing serviced land. If our province acts, and the city provides the necessary serviced land, it will remove one of the chief obstacles in our housing program.
Since the war, the city of Edmonton has made commitments by way of land subsidies and tax subsidies to the wartime housing amounting to over $2 million. The new scheme provides for government-sponsored housing schemes, whether for sale or rent, paying full municipal taxes. This remedies an injustice and removes a heavy financial burden which has been placed on many cities across Canada. The minister is to be highly commended for his very constructive proposals. I was pleased to hear his statement that the government does not propose to enter the construction field directly. The conditions I have described as pertaining to Edmonton could be duplicated to a greater or lesser degree in practically every city in Canada.

During the depression of the thirties, the house-building industry practically went out of existence. There were many technical advances during that time such as insulation, modern plumbing fixtures and improved heating equipment. Many new techniques were developed; but, because of depressed economic conditions, it made little difference so far as the general public was concerned. The introduction of the National Housing Act brought about a general improvement in many provinces. The reduction in the interest rate at that time was a big help. The difference between 4J per cent and 7 per cent, which was formerly the prevailing rate, on a $6,000 house means a saving of over $2,600 within a twenty-five year period.
Upon the outbreak of war the entire building industry was mobilized for war purposes. Barracks and emergency housing for war workers were built. These were produced at a speed which was thought impossible. There were, however, few private homes built until about 1944. The manufacturing and lumbering industries were still geared for war production and therefore many bottlenecks developed in the supply of building materials. Many of these scarcities have been with us until recently. It is only within the last few months that an adequate supply of building materials has been available. A high level of prosperity caused by the war and by wise government policy, contrary to the prophets of gloom, has been continued since the end of the war. It is without precedent and our economy still shows little sign of a recession. Our country is more prosperous than ever before in its history. More people are gainfully employed than at any time in our history. Our national income has more than doubled. The result is that the marriage rate is at an all-time high. Our housing industry has made a marvellous recovery since the war. We in Canada have produced more housing units, on a per capita basis, than has Great Britain or the United States. Nevertheless we have been barely keeping up with new family formations. There has been a vast improvement in the quality of housing during the last twenty years. The house of today is insulated, and is fully equipped with modern kitchen, bathroom and efficient heating equipment. In the short period of five years there has been a tremendous technical improvement both in materials and in contractors' equipment, and also in the planning of homes. The home of today is planned for use rather than for appearances. Costs are high, but I do not think anyone can successfully refute the statement that the general public today are better able to pay for housing than they ever before have been.

I do not believe that the average person in this country wants subsidies. All that the young people want is a chance to help themselves. Shelter is one of the necessities of life. We cannot escape it. We pay for the landlord's house or we pay for our own. The monthly carrying charges for a home under the National Housing Act, including principal, interest and taxes, is in most cases less than the rent for similar accommodatioii. Every payment adds to the purchaser's estate and in a few years he has become a home owner with all the advantages of a more satisfactory family life, which is reflected in the community life. I believe the new legislation will provide a solution to most of the problems besetting the industry, recognizing of course the fact that public subsidies may be necessary for those who, because of age, infirmity or extreme misfortune, are unable to help themselves. I am confident that if we are to accomplish the maximum production of housing necessary to provide decent shelter for all of the Canadian people, it can only be accomplished through the co-operation of the industry in all its branches, with all the governments, municipal, provincial and federal, participating.
Having regard to the greatly improved material and labour supply, I am confident that the industry, with the co-operation of the various governments, will during the next building season produce houses on a scale that was heretofore impossible. I hope to have a chance to speak on this housing bill when it is introduced, and I shall not take up more time at the present moment.
Before closing, I should like to say just a word about national unity. I am happy to be a member in this twenty-first parliament of Canada. During this parliament Canada will assume the full status of nationhood. With the inclusion of Newfoundland our family is complete. We have been greatly enriched, both materially and culturally. The spirit of true Canadianism which is personified in our esteemed Prime Minister is evident everywhere in Canada. Under his leadership I am confident that we are going forward to true national unity such as we have never before known. It is a privilege indeed to be here and to participate in the conduct of the national affairs of this country.

With the exception of the former Prime Minister, and I believe the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), who came to the house about the same time, I believe Mr. Senn was the senior member. I am pleased to have many inquiries concerning his health. These inquiries come from every part of the house, and they are deeply appreciated. I shall convey your good wishes to him, and I know they will make him very happy indeed. I am pleased to report that his health is slightly improved and that he continues to watch with keen interest the proceedings of the House of Commons.
This evening I intend to say a few words with respect to the question of markets, in which farming people throughout the country are keenly interested. I have received many communications from farmers across Canada concerning this vital subject. Therefore with Your Honour's permission I shall take a few moments of the time of the house to discuss the matter.
We have read in the press and heard over the air in the past few months a great deal of comment about future markets for our agricultural products. We hope to hear from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) before this debate is concluded just what our primary producers may expect in the way of markets in 1950.
During the ten-year period from 1939, our agricultural production in Canada was greatly accelerated. This was directly due to world war conditions, and as such it is only reason-

able to expect some reduction in demand as European countries come back into production.
As the hon. member for Frontenac-Adding-ton (Mr. Aylesworth) so ably brought to the attention of the house on April 27 of this year, the future outlook for Canadian agricultural markets appears to have receded beyond what many consider to be in the best interests of this country, and this very basic Canadian industry. During the ten-year period from 1939, we negotiated with the United Kingdom over 140 agreements for the purchase of various agricultural products. Today there are only four in existence, namely, wheat, bacon, cheese, eggs; and, with the exception of wheat, these are for very considerably reduced amounts.
While these agreements were in force, the price was in many instances below the prevailing world price, if such could accurately be determined, and at any rate was certainly competitive with what the same products could be purchased for elsewhere. During those years, little objection was expressed to the policy of selling to the United Kingdom below what was considered a world price, because it was hoped that by so doing we would retain these markets for our Canadian farmers after the war was over and when competition would become more keen.
These contracts also served as the support for farm prices in this country. Today that prop is rapidly disappearing. No indication has been given as yet whether or not the three remaining- agreements, in addition to the wheat agreement, will be renewed after this year.
The Financial Post, in a dispatch by their own special correspondent who reported the Washington conference, stated in a story published on September 17 last:
It is considered unlikely that Britain will renew her 1949 contracts for Canadian eggs, bacon and cheese.
While this may not mean that the United Kingdom will discontinue buying any or all of these items from Canada, it very clearly indicates that we can expect substantially reduced United Kingdom markets in 1950. Should such a situation actually materialize, it would be very serious for our Canadian farmers.
Our bacon contract for 1949 was for 160 million pounds, representing a very considerable reduction from the contract year 1945-46, when we shipped in excess of a billion pounds to the United Kingdom market.
This bacon market which Canadian farmers hoped to retain after the war has been reduced from year to year, until today it is a matter of question how much of this

market Canada will retain. Some months ago, Britain's food minister stated that the United Kingdom intended to purchase all the bacon, eggs, et cetera, that countries such as Denmark, Poland and Hungary could sell to them. This announced change of policy was followed by agreements for bacon with a number of countries including Denmark, Poland and Hungary, over periods of four and five years, extending up to 1953.
Since these agreements have been negotiated, giving these European countries a good portion of the British bacon market, other factors have arisen which may result in reduced sales of Canadian bacon in the United Kingdom market.
Similar uncertainty exists in connection with our United Kingdom market for cheese, our present contracts for 50 million pounds representing an amount lower than our shipments to this market in any one of the last fifty years.
Today, United Kingdom markets, formerly supplied by Canada, are being filled elsewhere under agreements negotiated within the past year. Australia and New Zealand now supply cheese under a contract which extends to 1955. Denmark, Holland, Switzerland and France have also in the last year become substantial suppliers of this commodity in the British market. Our present market for eggs expires this coming January. Last year this contract was reduced by 38 per cent from the adjusted 1948 figure. Since that time, under the bilateral trade agreements which the United Kingdom negotiated with European and other countries, Poland, Denmark, Holland, Eire, and Australia have all become suppliers in this market under contracts, one of which, with Poland, extends until 1954.
Is it any wonder that our farmers are concerned about future United Kingdom markets for these and other agricultural products? This concern, which is very widely felt, arises not alone from what has happened to these contracts in the past few years, but largely from indications of what the future may hold.
Some months ago the United Kingdom announced its intention to cut purchases from the dollar area by one quarter. Has the Minister of Agriculture yet been able to ascertain whether or not this announced policy to reduce imports by one quarter will apply to the few remaining or existing food contracts?
Just recently, I noticed a press report to the effect that the United Kingdom officials had informed the continuing committee on Anglo-Canadian trade that the recent devaluation of sterling will have little immediate bearing on previous intentions to cut purchases in the dollar area by one-quarter.
The Address-Mr. Catherwood
Since the United Kingdom announced its intention to cut imports from the dollar area, a five-year trade pact with Czechoslovakia has been signed, amounting to $340 million, including foodstuffs and other goods that in the past came chiefly from Canada and the United States.
It is also reported that the United Kingdom is at present negotiating trade agreements with Yugoslavia, Hungary and Russia, all of which involves goods, chiefly primary products, formerly purchased from Canada.
These new trade agreements, along with bilateral deals now in existence with Poland, Denmark, Hungary, Russia and other countries, constitute a threat, and a very serious threat, to the future markets, particularly of the primary producers of this country.
During the past ten years our food contracts with Britain have, with the exception of wheat, been largely for periods of one year. Contracts with other countries such as Poland, Denmark, Holland, Czechoslovakia and other countries, have been for periods of up to five years. While there may have been some advantage in annual negotiation of these contracts, the fact remains that we now find ourselves with a very materially reduced number of contracts, all but one of which expire at the end of this crop year.
Today we enter into the question of new contracts, at a time when the United Kingdom has negotiated bilateral deals with several countries for the supply of primary products formerly purchased from Canada. In addition to this there is the question of price. Many of these countries which today have long-term bilateral agreements with the United Kingdom have devaluated their currency in close relationship to the devaluation of the British pound. As a result, our ability to sell in the United Kingdom markets will have to meet competition not only from the many bilateral deals now in existence, but as well from the question of price and any advantage which may accrue to these European countries as a result of devaluation.
I bring this matter to the attention of the house at this time in the hope that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will at the earliest opportunity make a statement to parliament and to the country as to the future outlook for agricultural markets.
I make this suggestion because I believe it to be in the interest of the farmers of this country who today face a crisis on the question of future markets, notwithstanding the fact that no cabinet minister has to date participated in this debate.
At the present time the situation is not as serious perhaps as the facts would indicate,

The Address-Mr. Welbourn but this in no way lessens the potential dangers ahead. The production of agricultural products is not something that can be turned off and on again like an electric switch. Our farmers require to know well in advance what possible markets exist in order that they may plan their year's production. Up to the present we have been able to sell much of our surplus production in the United States of America and this has served to defer the crisis which otherwise would have arisen as a result of markets lost in the United Kingdom.
Today we can no longer ignore the fact that we have a similarity of production with the United States and indicated surpluses in that country no longer provide our farmers with any assurance of markets in that direction.
In the past our food contracts with the United Kingdom have been a prop for prices in Canada. The question now is: Will the existing contracts be renewed, and at what price? Is there any prospect or possibility of regaining for the farmers of this country markets in the United Kingdom for those goods which we supplied in such large quantities during the past ten years?
The speech from the throne indicates:
The government is seeking by all appropriate neans to co-operate in measures to restore economic equilibrium. The achievement of a pattern of world trade in which the trading nations can operate together within one single multilateral system continues to be the ultimate aim of my government.
I hope that the minister will take these facts into consideration, because these things are of vital concern to our farming people, and I hope also that the minister will be in position to advise this house and the people of Canada at the earliest possible date so that the farmers of Canada may know just what to expect in the future in regard to markets.

The constituency of Jasper-Edson, which I have the honour to represent, is in my opinion the finest constituency in Canada. Situated as it is in the west central part of Alberta, it extends from just outside the outskirts of the city of Edmonton for a distance of 275 miles west to the boundary of British Columbia. Jasper-Edson is bounded on the south by the Saskatchewan river and it extends north to Chisholm Mills on the Athabasca river.
In the east and northeastern parts of the constituency we have some of the finest agricultural land in western Canada, admirably suited to mixed farming and the growing of grass, clover and alfalfa seed. I speak from personal knowledge of this area as my father homesteaded a few miles west of Edmonton in the year 1892, and in that particular area there has never to this date been a crop failure. Also in the constituency immediately west of Edmonton is located the Wood-bend oil fields with the now world famous Schoepp No. 1 well which has the greatest depth of oil-bearing strata ever found in an oil well. This is just seven miles from my old farm. Crude oil from this field is flowing by pipe line, truck and tank cars to the various refineries in western Canada.
In the central part of the riding there are vast areas of timber where millions of feet of lumber and many hundreds of thousands of ties are cut every year. In this area as well are deposits of coal that are apparently inexhaustible and on the coal branch the very finest grades of steam and domestic coal are produced. I read in a recent Ottawa paper that coal, advertised as American coal, is being sold here in Ottawa at $24 to $25 per ton and yet a few months ago one of the old established mines at Mountain Park closed down because of lack of orders for their products. I would urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) to give serious consideration to the problem of devising ways and means of placing western coal in the bins of the consumers in this part of the dominion.

There are several well developed summer resorts in Jasper-Edson. The Seba and Kapasiwin beaches on lake Wabamun and Alberta beach on lac Ste. Anne are all within easy driving range of Edmonton and are patronized very extensively by the residents of that city. In the two lakes I have just mentioned, as well as in other lakes in that area, commercial fishing is an industry that brings a very substantial revenue to the residents of the constituency. The whitefish that are taken from the waters of lake Wabamun are recognized as the finest in Canada.
We all know and appreciate the value of tourist traffic to the economy of this country. In fact it has developed into one of the greatest industries in Canada, and in Jasper national park we have an attraction for tourists that is second to none in the dominion.
The town of Jasper is situated in a valley surrounded by towering snow-covered mountains, with many lakes and streams, well stocked with trout. It forms a setting that many tourists return to year after year. Adequate accommodation is provided both at Jasper Park lodge, the modern hotels in the town of Jasper and many attractive bungalow cabins. The dominion government maintains a large and up-to-date fish hatchery in Jasper for the purpose of restocking the lakes and streams to provide sport for the tourists. The number of tourists visiting Jasper park has been increasing steadily each year, and nearly twice as many visited there in 1949 as in the previous year. The number of tourists will be very greatly increased if and when there is a suitable surfaced road leading to and Erom Jasper park. He said: Mr. Speaker, a bill identical to this was introduced two sessions ago, in the last parliament, and was adopted. It had to do with the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company, which carries on operations in Manitoba and Saskatchewan; and for very obvious reasons the house saw fit to adopt that legislation.
The purpose of this bill is quite simple. As I said when introducing the legislation, the purpose is to bring the meat packing industry under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act so that if a dispute should occur with respect to any matter of collective bargaining, the federal Department of Labour will have power to step in and try to conciliate the dispute. The department has done this in the past; it has been very successful in its endeavours, and deserves much credit for what it has achieved.
The meat packing industry is of importance to all Canadians; it is important to the workers in industry, to the producers who supply the livestock, and of course to all of us as consumers. I suppose most hon. members remember the last strike that took place in the industry, in 1947. On that occasion two groups suffered most: the workers, through loss of income, and the producers who also suffered a loss of income because they were unable to market their livestock. That dispute began with Swift Canadian Limited, and it continued for two weeks. Had the federal department had the power to intervene, I am quite sure this dispute could have been settled. As it was, it lingered on for two weeks and then spread throughout the industry. In no small measure, settlement was delayed by the refusal of Swift Canadian to arbitrate the dispute, in spite of their being requested to do so by the Canadian Federation of Agricul-

Meat Packing Industry ture and various provincial governments. While I have said the workers and producers suffered during that strike, according to the evidence submitted to the prices committee it would appear that the companies did not do so badly in the long run, for they made more money in the two months following the strike than they made in the previous eight months. The reason for that is fairly obvious; there was a glut of livestock on the market, and we had a population which to a certain extent was meat starved.
There are three major meat packing companies in Canada: Canada Packers, Burns and Swift Canadian. The policies of these three companies are directed from their head offices. I have no quarrel at all with that; but that being so, of course the union had to constitute itself in such a way that it could deal efficiently with the employers; so the bargaining powers of the union also are concentrated. Bargaining on a national basis was first accepted in 1944, when there was a dispute in the meat packing industry. At that time the federal Department of Labour stepped into the picture under the War Measures Act and appointed a conciliation commissioner, who assisted in no small measure in the settlement of the dispute. The same thing happened in 1945 and in 1946, when the federal department was able to bring about an amicable settlement. In 1947 jurisdiction over most labour matters was returned to the provinces, and we had a different situation. While the united packing-house workers were continuing to deal with the employers on a national scale, because of provincial jurisdiction there was no national authority to which they could apply for help in arriving at a settlement. The union, therefore, was compelled to go to eight different provinces with the inevitable result. - It would be almost as logical to expect the railway brotherhoods to go to the eight provinces to find some amicable settlement in one of their disputes. I am certain that this unworkable situation was in no small way a cause of the 1947 strike and of the undue delay in settlement.
If negotiations on a national scale fail to resolve differences, there is no provision for conciliation at the top level today. As I say, conciliation has to take place through the various provincial governments if any settlement is to be reached, The consequences are as obvious as they are serious. Today, in its agreement with two of the major companies, Canada Packers and Burns, the union has a clause containing a provision for the mediation of disputes before a strike vote is taken. Thus, we see the industry recognizes the need for national collective bargaining, and believes it to be the most effective

way of bargaining. Past experience has shown that peaceful settlements can be reached on a national scale, whereas on a provincial scale there has been conflict, with eventual strikes. No one, of course, wants to see that. The differences between the union and the companies in 1944-45 were much greater than those which exist today. If the federal Department of Labour could bring about a peaceful settlement of these differences, then I am convinced it could do so now if workable machinery could be made available for use in the event of a breakdown of negotiations. Agreements would then be reached quickly and efficiently. If that happens, then Canada will be spared the expense as well as the annoyance of a strike in this important industry. It is for that reason I am anxious to see this industry placed under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. I am certain the results would be of benefit and to the general advantage of Canada as a whole. (Translation):

Efforts were made, even during the last election, to bring the people to believe that provincial autonomy would be in danger if the Liberal party were returned to power. But, as was seen, the great majority of the people did not believe those false prophets and showed by a nearly unanimous vote, that they had full and complete confidence, on this point, in the honesty of our distinguished leader, the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and of his candidates.

speechtext:
The objections, Mr. Speaker, to the bill which has been proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) are extremely simple and obvious, and they have an importance which has nothing to do with the question of the relationship between employers and employees in the meat packing industry in Canada or in any other industry. The bill proposed by the hon. member is to amend section 53 of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, an act to provide for the investigation, conciliation and settlement of industrial disputes, assented to on June 30, 1948, and which is chapter 54 of the Statutes of Canada, 1948.
When we read the section which it is proposed to amend, we see the real objection to the amendment proposed. Section 53 is the section which deals with the application of the act, and it reads as follows:
Part I of this act shall apply in respect of employees who are employed upon or in connection with the operation of any work, undertaking or business that is within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada including, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing-
And then are set out certain subsections which delineate certain of the undertakings or businesses within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada to which the

Meat Packing Industry act applies. The purpose of the amendment is to add, by declaration of this parliament, a certain business or undertaking as a work for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more provinces.
As this country is a federal state, there are certain limitations upon the legislative authority of this parliament, and they are those set out in our constitution, the British North America Act, which lays down a division of authority between this parliament and the legislatures of the various provinces. When we say that there is a limitation upon the power of this parliament, that does not mean that this parliament is not free to pass any sort of legislation which it may see fit to pass; but there is a limitation on the effectiveness of that legislation by reason of the fact that if this parliament sees fit to pass an act which infringes upon, or tries to take away any of the authority which, by the constitution, is given to the provinces, that act is ineffective in spite of the fact that it is passed by this parliament because it will be declared ultra vires when submitted to the courts. We are therefore free to pass an amendment of this kind if we see fit to do so; but by so doing we cannot make it effective. Therefore, in reviewing any legislation which comes before it, it is one of the responsibilities of this parliament to see that such legislation is within its competence. Otherwise, in passing it we are doing an empty act, something which will in the end be found to be completely ineffective.
In the field of relationships between employers and employees in this country, the parliament of Canada is competent to deal with matters for which no better description exists than that which is contained in the preamble of section 53, which I have already read, namely, matters within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada. If a matter is not within our legislative authority, Mr. Speaker, we cannot effectively pass any legislation dealing with it.

speechtext:
If it was by consent, then the provinces withdrew. That is a different situation. I do not think there has been any suggestion that any consent had been given by the provinces to the amendment that has been proposed by my hon. friend.
But, Mr. Speaker, that is the situation in the field of labour relations. The preamble of this section is the operative part of it. Hon. members who were members of the industrial relations committee of the last parliament which considered the clauses of this bill will recall that when this particular section was before the committee it was in a slightly different form from that in which it now appears in the bill. The preamble was shorter, and the provision with respect to the limitation "within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada" appeared as one of the subsections of the suggested section.
The section as it then stood was thoroughly discussed in the committee and on the motion of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) it was amended. The amendment was agreed to by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), and the section was redrafted in the form in which it now stands. As the result of the present form of the section, the operative words "within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada" affect the whole meaning of the following subsections of the section, and these subsections are merely in the act to indicate the various activities which are within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, either by direct legislative authority in the constitution or as a result of judicial decision in constitutional cases where the provisions of the constitution, the British North America Act, have been interpreted. The various matters are there set out. The proposal is to add to these matters the particular industry of meat packing.
The situation is this, Mr. Speaker. Whether or not this house sees fit to pass the proposed amendment, it will not in itself put the meat packing industry, or any other industry, within the legislative capacity of the parliament of Canada. I personally do not think it can reasonably be argued that the meat packing industry is an industry which should come under the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada as opposed to the provinces, any more than a half dozen other industries that one could name, for example, the creamery industry or the farming industry, or any industry that is carried on in the majority of the provinces of this country.
I submit that in passing this amendment we would be doing an act which would be

found in the result to be completely ineffective, and we would be found to have attempted to legislate in a field which is closed to us by the constitution. I think that is the most important aspect of this question.
The relationships between the central government and the provinces are matters which have to be dealt with with great care, and this parliament should not knowingly and intentionally infringe upon any of the legislative fields which have been assigned to the provinces, without the consent of the provinces affected. We have heard a great deal, not only in this session but during the last session, about provincial rights and consultation with the provinces. This is clearly a case where the passage of this amendment would be an infringement of provincial rights, the invasion by this parliament of a field which has always been clearly understood to be within provincial jurisdiction
The arguments which were made by the hon. member in introducing his bill may well be arguments which should be considered by a body which is representative of all the parties concerned and is dealing with the question of amendment of the constitution or of assigning to the central government, the federal parliament, certain powers, which under modern conditions it needs. But the fact is that the federal parliament has not now the authority to invade this field, and without the consent of those who have the field I submit that we have no right to invade it.
Perhaps the hon. member will have an opportunity to make his submissions to a body which will consider the arguments he has put forward, apart from their connotation in this instance. I submit, however, that this parliament has to consider its position as a legislative body with restricted powers and the responsibility, greater perhaps than it might have had even in the immediate past, of seeing that we do nothing which might be interpreted as an intentional and complete invasion of a field which has been dealt with by the provinces in the past. Mr. Speaker, we are now considering a bill introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) to amend section 53 of the act appearing in statute 1112 George VI, chapter 54, and entitled "The Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act". That title is so clear that it speaks for itself.
Section 53, which the bill would amend, contains the very provisions designed to determine the administration of the act.
The proposed amendment would broaden the scope of the act to include certain packing houses and related industries which would then come under the sole authority of the federal government in matters of industrial relations and disputes.
Mr. Speaker, if I may use a familiar phrase, everyone should stick to his trade. I do not propose to question, at this stage, the advisability of the bill under review. I know that the matter of the strike in the packing industry will be brought up. If, however, I were to venture upon this ground I would only be heading for disaster. In my humble opinion, at first glance, this legislation may appear restricted in its scope, but it could establish a precedent whose full implications I am at the moment unable to foresee.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that this section 53, which it is proposed to amend, is worth reading. It will be found to be an almost textual reproduction of the terms of the constitution, that is the British North America Act, 1867, especially paragraph (g) of section 53, which reads as follows:
(g) such works or undertakings as, although wholly within a province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces',
That should be compared with the following paragraph (c) of subsection 10 of section 92 of the B.N A. Act. But first, so that we may have a better understanding of the text, I quote the heading of subsection 10, as follows:
10. Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes:
And paragraph (c):
(c) Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
We must therefore conclude that the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act is couched in such terms, the very terms of the constitution, that it is intra vires in that it scrupulously respects the rights of the provinces in matters of this nature. I

Meat Packing Industry submit, humbly but with the utmost conviction, that the separation of legislative powers is one of the keystones of our constitution. To me it would be rash to invade this field unless every precaution which human wisdom can foresee had been taken.
I admit that paragraph (c) of subsection 10 of section 92 of the British North America Act which I have just quoted could, after summary consideration, provide an easy and expeditious solution. I feel, however, that the remedy suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North is worse than the evil he is trying to cure.
This is a rather strange fact, but I believe I can vouch for its absolute veracity: the provisions of paragraph (c) of subsection 10 of section 92 were never resorted to when our country was faced with the many problems which the conduct of the war brought to our attention with an impatience that would tolerate no delay. If the federal government invaded legislative fields belonging to the provinces, it did so when faced by the imminent danger of war by referring to section 91 of the constitution. I am prepared to admit, for the sake of discussion, that it may be that the federal authority is better prepared than are the provincial governments to deal, for instance, with certain labour disputes. However, it would be necessary to investigate the devices to be sought in an agreement with the provinces. But deliberately, in one fell swoop, might I say, to assume a legislative power hitherto exercised by the provinces would not only be high-handed but, to my mind, at a time when precisely there are disputes regarding the separation of legislative powers between the federal government and the various provincial governments, it would be provocative. Nay, it would be setting fire to the powder kegs.
Not for a moment, Mr. Speaker, do I wish to impugn the good faith of the member from Winnipeg North; not for a moment would I gainsay the commendability of his intentions. However, being a Liberal, I attach great importance to provincial autonomy and I therefore feel it to be my duty to warn the house against this bill whose surest and almost inevitable effect would be to create a dangerous precedent which, in time to come, would provide the federal government with a convenient means to gather unto itself legislative powers which the constitution has reserved exclusively to the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I am wondering why, with the inadequate means at my disposal, I have made so bold as to take part in this debate.
I have found the means to do so in my conviction that the Liberal creed has as a basic tenet a claim to total autonomy for the


national government in its own field and, at the same time, a claim to complete autonomy for the provinces. That is why I wish to warn the house against adopting this amendment which would create a precedent through which, I believe, the autonomy of the provinces would be forever threatened. I feel sure that in wishing to improve a certain state of affairs, the member for Winnipeg North has not considered all the consequences of his amendment. I would therefore ask him not to give up the object which he has in view, but to choose some other method whereby, while achieving it, he will not be creating the precedent which would otherwise follow its approval by this house.

Mr. Speaker, I did not have the pleasure of hearing the remarks of the hon. member who introduced this bill, but I think I can agree that the reasons for its introduction are perfectly legitimate and proper, that is, if the hon. member wants the labour laws of this country to be uniform as far as they affect those great industries which employ large numbers of work people. If that is his object, and I think it is, then I am in hearty agreement with him. The time has come, as a matter of fact it has long passed, when something should be done, either by amending the British North America Act or through other legislation, to give the Department of Labour at Ottawa jurisdiction in connection with labour difficulties and other labour matters affecting the large industries in this country, especially those which operate in more than one province.
I remember when I was chairman of a committee of this house which sat some years
Meat Packing Industry ago. Another member of that committee was a gentleman who has since passed away. He was a gentleman for whom I had the highest regard and I think he had some regard for me after we became acquainted. For years the provincial governments of our provinces -I refer to both Liberal and Conservative governments-had taken the stand, when a labour union or a group of men went to them to ask for the passage of laws with regard to the hours of labour in a particular industry, that that was a matter for the dominion parliament. Then when they would come to the dominion parliament they would be told that hours of labour and that sort of thing were matters over which the provincial legislatures had jurisdiction. Both governments were right, but the unfortunate thing was that the labour people of this country were led around for years in connection with the eight-hour day.
The late Mr. Woodsworth brought these facts to the attention of our committee and one of the recommendations of that committee was that a case be presented to the Supreme Court of Canada. Anyone who knew anything about the law knew what the law was, but there was a need to define the jurisdiction of the dominion and the provinces in connection with hours of labour. Unfortunately the minister of labour of that time combined with that reference a reference concerning matters which were under consultation at the Geneva conference. There was never any doubt that jurisdiction rested with the provincial legislatures concerning local matters and with this parliament concerning dominion matters such as railroads and so on.
I do not know whether the hon. gentleman who spoke last is a lawyer, but I am in agreement with him. I submit that this parliament has the jurisdiction to pass the bill introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North. That power is given to this parliament by section 92, subsection 10, paragraph (c) of the British North America Act, which the hon. gentleman quoted. But even though this legislation is enacted I doubt if it would meet the intentions of the hon. member who has introduced it.
Section 92 outlines the exclusive powers of the legislatures of the provinces. The subsection quoted by the hon. gentleman gives this parliament the power to pass this legislation, but this parliament would have no right to hand over any civil rights. That cannot be done when it is purely a question of civil rights. There is another section in the British North America Act which I have often thought should be more widely used. I refer to section 94, which reads:

Meat Packing Industry
Notwithstanding anything in this act, the parliament of Canada may make provision for the uniformity of all or any of the laws relative to property and civil rights in Ontario, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick, and of the procedure of all or any of the courts in those three provinces, and from and after the passing of any act in that behalf the power of the parliament of Canada to make laws in relation to any matter comprised in any such act shall, notwithstanding anything in this act, be unrestricted; but any act of the parliament of Canada making provision for such uniformity shall not have effect in any province unless and until it is adopted and enacted as law by the legislature thereof.
After this act was passed there were four provinces; but the province of Quebec is not included under the act. In other words the province of Quebec was not given power even to adopt the laws on property and civil rights that might be passed and handed on by the parliament of Canada. There was very good reason for that. The civil law of the province of Quebec was not the same as the civil law of the other provinces, at least at that time.
When I was in this house previously, so many years ago that if I were to tell you how long you would think I was a decrepit old man, I had hopes of getting this parliament to pass legislation on civil rights as far as they concern labour, which would afford the provinces an opportunity of accepting and adopting those laws. In other words, I would have had parliament pass the law and let the provinces adopt it if they wished. It was always pointed out that after all this would not be such legislation as the creators of the British North America Act had in view, though I do not agree with that contention. Today, however, I believe it is still open to the parliament of Canada to pass a general labour law and let the provinces adopt that law if they wish to do so. Of course Quebec could not do that, because under the British North America Act it was not given power to adopt such legislation.
I am not opposing the principle of this bill, but I think the time must come when legislation will have to be passed to make the labour laws of this country uniform, not only with regard to the meat packing industry or any other special industry but with regard to all large industries that have their location in more than one province. That would be fair to labour and fairer still, I think, to industry if only they would look at it in the right way, though of course I do not know how they would look at legislation of this kind. But even if this parliament passed this bill tonight, I do not think we would achieve the purpose the hon. member has in mind. We have the jurisdictional power to pass such legislation. That is given in the very labour code which has been adopted by this house.
Paragraph (g) of section 53 cites verbatim the very words quoted by my hon. friend from the British North America Act. So I do not think there can be any doubt that parliament has the power, as far as legislative jurisdiction is concerned, to pass a bill of this kind tonight or any other time.
As I say, however, I do not believe the adoption of such legislation would meet the purpose-and it is a very good purpose-of the hon. gentleman who introduced the legislation. I do not think that would produce what he wants to produce. If the time comes when this government will undertake to consult the provinces in regard to matters over which the legislatures have jurisdiction in order to bring about some compromise, and if I am in this house, I shall be one hundred per cent behind the hon. member and others who may support such legislation. At the proper time I shall certainly be in favour of legislation that will bring all large industries doing business in more than one province under the jurisdiction of our labour code.
